chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 51 to 60, the friend's speech decade of the marutham hundred: the friend faces the straying husband, calling him home to a pregnant wife, asking at whose door his chariot stands, laying the girl's sickness to his broken oath, measuring her fading beauty by the rich towns of the Pandya, the Chola and Viraan, mocking his rival woman, grieving that she who once cured his love has no cure for the wife, and in the last poem warning a night visitor of the father's spear.

51.reading: The friend tells the lord of the town where the sharp-clawed hen of the blue water-cock has her pregnancy cravings that this girl's craving is not a longing for sour tamarind but a sickness that only his opened chest will cure.
51.nuance: The town epithet already shows a pregnant bird with her mate; the friend then sets the woman's craving against the bird's and names the cure as the husband's embrace, so the pregnancy becomes her claim on a man who is elsewhere. The usual craving of pregnant women for tart fruit is denied in order to say what she really wants.

thinai_evidence.note: a water-fowl of the fields and the lord of a town

comparisons.tenor: the girl's pregnancy craving, which is for his chest and not for sour fruit

52.reading: The friend asks the man, while the young girl with red mouth and red-lined rain-wet eyes grieves, her red fingers stained from weaving garlands of the red vayalai creeper, in front of which house his chariot now stands.
52.nuance: The poem is built in red: the creeper, her fingers, her eyes reddened by weeping, her mouth; the one question at the end points to the houses of other women without naming them. The girl is still young enough to be playing with creeper garlands.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's chariot at another door and the wife's grief, the uri of marutham

53.reading: The friend asks the lord of the town of ponds, where the field lotus blooms though stirred muddy when the new flood breaks the dam and pours in, why anyone should think the ford's spirit afflicts them: the sickness they suffer is the oath he swore.
53.nuance: The household's diagnosis is possession by the deity of the ford (துறை அணங்கும்); the friend replaces it with his broken oath, which was presumably sworn at that ford. The flood that breaks its bank and the lotus that blooms though muddied invite a hidden reading (his broken bound, her troubled faithfulness), but only one pair is clear, so it stays scene. Line 3 recurs in Ainkurunuru 94.

54.reading: The friend tells the man, as this girl who is like Tenur in the Pandya's good land, where cool water flows even in summer, finds her chosen bangles slipping, that she fears for the girls in sedge garlands who came because he brought them, should their turn come too.
54.nuance: The fear is not for the wife but for the new women: what has happened to her will happen to them in its order (அம்முறை). The Pandya's town that never runs dry is the measure of the beauty that has now run dry in her. The construction of lines 4 to 6 is uncertain (ஊரின் ஊரனை, and whom the man 'brought').

55.reading: The friend tells the man that because he desired this girl's fine beauty and then left her, she who is like Tenur of the chariot-giving lord, where the sugarcane press roars back at the elephants, now has a brow gone pale for many to see.
55.nuance: பல்லோர் அறிய makes the pallor public: it is evidence against him in the town, not only her private suffering. The noisy cane-press answering the elephants gives Tenur the sound of plenty, set against the silent sign on her brow.

56.reading: The friend asks the man what use his reassuring words are, now that the bright brow of this girl, who is like the war-winning Cholas' Amur, where lamps that hold off the day's end leave no night known, has faded.
56.nuance: The town that never knows night because its lamps burn on is matched to a brow called சுடர்நுதல், a brow that gives light; its dimming (தேம்ப) is the one fact the man's words cannot argue away.

57.reading: The friend asks the man whether his woman has beauty to match this girl's, who is like Tenur with its fields of water lilies that glow in daylight like a many-rayed fire, that he leaves her beauty to languish alone.
57.nuance: The question is mocking: the friend assumes no rival can equal her, so his leaving can only be folly. நின் பெண்டே turns the other woman into his, with the wife left without a word for herself.

58.reading: The friend tells the man that he looks like one seized by this girl's beauty, she who is like Iruppai of generous-handed Viraan, where stacks of white paddy stand like mountains; yet he keeps house for others, long may he live.
58.nuance: அணங்கு உற்றனை போறி is ironic: he acts the possessed lover here while his household is elsewhere (பிறர்க்கு மனையையால்); the closing blessing வாழி நீயே is said in scorn.

59.reading: The friend asks the man to listen: she who once became the medicine that ended the pain of his love-mad heart now grieves in her own heart that she can be no medicine for this girl.
59.nuance: The friend recalls her old part as go-between in the secret love, when she cured him by bringing them together; now that he has strayed, the same friend has no cure for the wife, so her service in kalavu turns into helplessness in karpu.

60.reading: The friend tells the lord of the field-town, where the water-hen in the pond calls its mate, that she will say it plainly: he comes again and again to the tall house while all are asleep; does he not fear the spear in this girl's father's hand?
60.nuance: A marutham poem with a kurinji situation: the night visit to an unmarried girl's house and the father's spear are the stock pressures of kalavu toward marriage. The water-hen calling openly to its mate in the field is set against the lover who comes by stealth at night.

iraicchi.sense: the bird calls its mate in the open, while the man comes to her only by stealth at night; he should claim her openly

links.note: Kuruntokai 53 names what afflicts them as the oath he swore at their town's ford, holding her forearm before the water goddesses; Ainkurunuru 53 has the friend ask why the ford should be blamed for their sickness when the cause is his oath.
links.teaches: Read together they show that the ford was both where the oath was sworn and where the household looked for the spirit that seized the girl, so the friend's correction turns the family's diagnosis of possession into a charge of perjury against the man.

links.note: In Kural 1183 the woman says he took her grace and modesty and gave her sickness and pallor in exchange; in Ainkurunuru 55 the friend tells the man that because he desired her beauty and left her, her brow has paled for many to see.
links.teaches: The Kural keeps the exchange of beauty for pallor as the woman's private complaint, while the Ainkurunuru friend turns the same exchange into public evidence held up to the man, so the pallor that is a lament in the couplet becomes an accusation in the town.

links.note: Both measure a woman's beauty by Iruppai of the generous Viraan: in Natrinai 350 the wife says she would let that old beauty perish rather than accept the straying man; in Ainkurunuru 58 the friend says he seems possessed by it yet keeps house for others.
links.teaches: The same rich town names the wife's beauty both as what the straying husband pretends to be captured by and as what the wife herself is ready to lose rather than take him back, so the marutham quarrel is fought over who holds that beauty as a claim.

links.note: Kural 1102 says the woman is herself the cure for the sickness she causes the man; in Ainkurunuru 59 the friend says she was once the cure for his love-sick heart but can be no cure for the girl now.
links.teaches: The couplet makes the beloved the only remedy for the man's love-sickness, but the Sangam friend shows a third person who served as that remedy by bringing them together, and who has none for the woman once he strays, so the cure flows only toward the man.

links.note: In Akananuru 162 the man tells his heart that he stood in a midnight storm at a corner of her father's tall house until the strict guards slackened; in Ainkurunuru 60 the friend tells the man that he comes to the tall house while all sleep and asks whether he does not fear her father's spear.
links.teaches: The danger at the father's tall house that the lover recounts to himself as proof of his devotion is the very thing the friend names to him as a reason to stop coming by night, so the same risk is a boast in his mouth and a demand for marriage in hers.

source_issues: 51-60: the colophon has no thurai; the decade title தோழி கூற்றுப் பத்து gives only the speaker, so every addressee and stage in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem and occasion words are null.
53 line 3 recurs as Ainkurunuru 94 line 4 (flagged by show); marked as written, a shared formula.
54 lines 4-6: the construction of ஊரின் ஊரனை and of whom the man brought is uncertain; the verse is marked uncertain.
55 line 1 and 59 line 1 are repaired readings (flagged by show); marked as repaired.
60 line 2: கழனியுரநின் should read கழனி ஊர நின் (vocative ஊர, the long vowel lost in the e-text).
60 line 3: துங்சுமனை is a misspelling of துஞ்சுமனை (ங் for ஞ்).
